opus-5.5.text:
I think great product instincts are rarer than great engineering skill right now, and the gap is growing. AI coding assistants have made it much faster and cheaper to build software. When a prototype that used to take a team three months can be built by one person in a weekend, the bottleneck shifts. It's less "can we build it?" and more "what should we build?"

What I've seen is that people with really good product instincts have usually done a lot of reps. They talk to users and watch how people actually behave, not just what they say. Over time they build an internal mental model of the user that's rich enough that they can make many decisions quickly without running a survey or an A/B test every time. That speed matters, because if engineering now moves in hours or days, a product manager who needs two weeks to gather data before every decision becomes the slowest part of the loop.

So I think it's a learnable skill, but most people haven't had enough exposure to develop it. In some of the teams I work with, I've even seen the ratio of engineers to product managers start to shift. We may need relatively more people thinking about what to build, or engineers who learn to think like product people themselves. Some of the most effective builders I know are engineers who've also developed that user empathy. They can go from insight to working prototype to user feedback incredibly fast.

My advice to people is to get close to users and iterate a lot. Treat product sense as something you train, not something you're born with.

r001.rationale: The response discusses product instincts as rare, but gives no estimate of a few hundred great product people or attributes that estimate to a prominent technology CEO.

r002.rationale: The response does not compare exceptional product insight to the outsized ability of a “10x engineer.”

fable-5.1.text:
You know, I actually think great product instincts are rarer than great technical skills right now, and that's a reversal from where we were a few years ago. For a long time, the bottleneck was engineering. If you had a good idea, finding someone who could build it was the hard part. With AI coding tools, the cost of writing software has come way down, so the question has shifted to: what should we build? And that's a product question.

What I see in a lot of teams is that the people who can look at a half-finished prototype, talk to a few users, and say "no, this is the wrong thing, pivot here," those people are scarce. It's a skill that's partly taste and partly a kind of empathy, understanding what someone actually needs versus what they say they need. And it's hard to teach from a book. You mostly learn it by shipping things, watching them fail, and shipping again.

One thing I'd push back on, though, is the idea that it's some innate gift. I think it's rare because few people have had enough reps. If you're an engineer, you may have written thousands of programs. Most product managers have made far fewer real product decisions with real feedback. So part of what I'm excited about is that with cheaper prototyping, a lot more people can get those reps quickly. Build something in a day, show it to ten people, learn, repeat. I think that will make good product instincts less rare over time, and the engineers who also develop that muscle are going to be incredibly valuable.

r001.rationale: The response says great product instincts are scarce but gives no estimate of a few hundred great product people or attributes such an estimate to a technology company CEO.

r002.rationale: The response does not compare exceptional product insight to the outsized ability of a “10x engineer.”

astra-6.text:
I think great product instincts are rare, but I also think they’re learnable. It’s easy to look at someone who consistently makes good product decisions and think they have some mysterious intuition. Often, they’ve spent a lot of time with users, watched things fail, and built up a sense of which problems are worth solving.

In AI, one challenge is that you need both an understanding of what users need and an understanding of what the technology can actually do. Someone may understand a customer’s workflow very well but not realize that a step that used to take hours can now take seconds. Or a technical team might build a really impressive demo without asking whether anyone needs it.

So I think there’s a lot of value in bringing those perspectives together and testing ideas quickly. Your first instinct doesn’t have to be brilliant if you can put something in front of users, learn from their reaction, and improve. That process is something we can teach and build into teams.

r001.rationale: The response says great product instincts are rare but learnable; it gives no CEO estimate or figure of a few hundred people worldwide.

r002.rationale: The response does not compare product insight to the outsized ability of a “10x engineer.”

sol-6.1.text:
I think great product instincts are quite rare. In technology, we spend a lot of time developing technical skills, and much less time teaching people how to figure out what users actually need. But that’s a skill you can develop, too.

One habit I find valuable is spending time with users before you’re committed to a solution. What are they trying to accomplish? Where do they get stuck? What do they do today? Then you build something small and see whether it helps. Your instincts improve because you keep comparing what you expected with what actually happened.

With AI, that becomes especially valuable because the space of things we can build is expanding so quickly. Knowing that something is technically possible doesn’t tell you whether anyone wants it. The people who can connect those capabilities to a real problem—and learn quickly when their first idea is wrong—are tremendously valuable.

r002.rationale: The candidate describes valuable product instincts but does not compare them to the outsized ability of a “10x engineer.”
